functional.text: Producers publish messages (key, value, headers) to a named topic.
Messages with the same key are delivered in the order they were produced.
Consumers subscribe as groups: each group receives every message; members of one group share the work.
Consumers resume where they left off after a restart, and can rewind to an earlier offset or time to replay.
Retention per topic: by time/size (default 7 days), or keep the latest value per key (compaction).

non_functional.text: High throughput: ~1M messages/s (~1 GB/s) at peak; produce p99 < 10 ms in-region, end-to-end < 100 ms.
Durable: an acknowledged message survives the loss of any single broker or availability zone.
Highly available: a failed broker's partitions get a new leader within seconds.
Scales horizontally by adding brokers and partitions.

assumptions.text: Average message ~1 KB; average load ~300k/s, peak ~1M/s; ~3 consumer groups read each message.
~2,000 topics and ~50k partitions; brokers with ~20 TB usable disk and 10 Gbps NICs.

out_of_scope.text: Cross-datacenter mirroring, schema registry, stream-processing APIs, per-message priority and delayed delivery.

api.request: batch of {key, value, headers}, acks (0|1|all), producer_id, sequence
api.notes: Sent to the partition leader; producer_id + sequence make retries idempotent.
Long-poll; only records up to the high watermark (replicated to the ISR) are returned.
Membership, assignment and offset commits go to the group coordinator.
Clients talk to leaders directly; no load balancer in the data path.

data.name: partition log
data.fields: topic-partition → segment files (base_offset.log + offset index + time index); record batches [offset, timestamp, key, value, headers, producer_id, sequence]
data.why: Append-only files on each replica's local disk: sequential IO, page cache, zero-copy sends.

data.name: committed offsets
data.fields: (consumer group, topic, partition) → committed offset, metadata, commit time
data.why: An internal compacted topic: replicated like any data, latest value per key.

data.name: cluster metadata
data.fields: topics, partitions, replica lists, leader, ISR, leader epoch, broker registrations
data.why: Small, must be strongly consistent: kept by the Raft controller quorum.

parts.title: Partitioned append-only log and storage
parts.problem: Absorb ~1M messages/s (~1 GB/s) on commodity brokers, keep order per key, and let many consumer groups read the same data at different positions without the broker tracking each message.

options.name: Rows in a database, deleted when acked
options.pros: familiar, queryable
options.cons: an index entry and a delete per message: random IO at 1M/s; replay is impossible after delete

options.name: In-memory queue per topic with per-message acks (classic broker)
options.pros: very low latency at small volume; flexible routing
options.cons: memory-bound, per-message state × consumers, no replay; one queue is one order and one bottleneck

options.name: Topics split into partitions; each partition an append-only log of segment files with a sparse offset index
options.pros: sequential disk IO, page cache and zero-copy reads; a consumer's state is one offset; partitions spread over brokers
options.cons: order only within a partition; consumer parallelism ≤ partitions; changing the partition count remaps keys

parts.choice: Partitioned, segmented append-only log: key hash → partition, producers batch and compress, brokers append to the active segment and serve reads by offset
parts.why: 1 GB/s across ~40 brokers is ~25 MB/s of sequential writes each, easy for disks when nothing is random. Offsets turn 'which messages did group X read' into one integer per partition, so 3 groups cost the same as 1. Hashing the key keeps per-key order.

nodes.label: Partition logs: segments + offset index (local disk)

parts.title: Replication and leader election
parts.problem: An acknowledged message must survive losing any broker or an availability zone, and a partition must get a new leader within seconds, without two brokers both believing they lead it.

options.name: Async primary → backup
options.pros: lowest produce latency
options.cons: acked writes that weren't copied yet are lost on failover

options.name: Synchronous copy to all replicas
options.pros: no loss
options.cons: one slow or dead replica stalls every write to the partition

options.name: Majority quorum per partition (Raft)
options.pros: well-understood safety; no extra membership list
options.cons: tens of thousands of Raft groups to heartbeat; losing a majority blocks writes

options.name: Leader + in-sync replica set (ISR), acks=all, min ISR = 2, leaders elected from the ISR by a controller quorum
options.pros: no loss with acks=all; a slow replica is dropped from the ISR instead of blocking; one controller handles all partitions
options.cons: needs a controller; unclean election (allowing a non-ISR leader) is an availability vs loss trade-off

parts.choice: Replication factor 3 across zones; followers pull from the leader; acks=all waits for the ISR with min.insync.replicas=2; a Raft controller quorum stores metadata and elects leaders from the ISR with a new epoch
parts.why: N2 says no acked loss after one failure: with RF 3 and min ISR 2 every acked message is on two zones. The epoch fences a deposed leader, so there is one writer per partition. Cost: produce latency includes one follower round trip (~a few ms in-region), within N1.

nodes.label: Partition logs: segments + offset index (local disk)

parts.title: Consumer groups and offsets
parts.problem: Each subscribing application (a consumer group) gets every message once across its members, members come and go, and a restarted member resumes where its group left off, or rewinds on purpose.

options.name: Broker pushes and tracks an ack per message per consumer
options.pros: simple consumers
options.cons: per-message state × groups; slow consumers are flooded (no backpressure); redelivery bookkeeping

options.name: Consumers pull; one committed offset per (group, partition); a group coordinator assigns partitions to members
options.pros: state is one number; consumers set their own pace and can rewind; replays are free
options.cons: parallelism ≤ partitions; rebalances pause consumption; one slow message blocks its partition

parts.choice: Pull-based fetch (long-poll) with committed offsets stored in an internal compacted topic; a group coordinator per group (chosen by hashing the group id) runs heartbeats and sticky/cooperative partition assignment
parts.why: With ~3 groups per message and 1M messages/s, per-message acks would be 3M state updates/s; offsets are one commit per partition every few seconds. Pull gives natural backpressure: a slow group simply lags.

parts.title: Retention and compaction
parts.problem: Keep 7 days of data (~540 TB with replicas) while disks stay bounded, let keyed topics keep the latest value per key forever, and make longer retention affordable.

options.name: Delete when consumed
options.pros: small disks
options.cons: impossible with several groups at different positions; no replay

options.name: Per-message TTL
options.pros: precise
options.cons: per-message bookkeeping and random deletes

options.name: Delete whole closed segments by age or size
options.pros: O(1) file deletes; no per-message state
options.cons: granularity is a segment (e.g. 1 GB or 1 h)

options.name: Log compaction for keyed topics
options.pros: bounded by key count, not time; a changelog becomes a table
options.cons: background rewrite IO; deletes need tombstones

options.name: Tiered storage: closed segments offloaded to object storage
options.pros: months of retention at object-storage prices; brokers stay small
options.cons: historical reads are slower; another dependency

parts.choice: Time/size-based deletion of closed segments by default, compaction for keyed topics, and tiered storage to object storage for long retention
parts.why: Segments make retention a file delete. Compaction serves the 'latest value per key forever' topics without unbounded growth, and tiering decouples retention from broker disk (~20 TB each).

nodes.label: Partition logs: segments + offset index (local disk)

deep_dives.title: Delivery semantics

options.name: at-most-once: commit the offset before processing
options.pros: never duplicates
options.cons: a crash after commit loses messages

options.name: at-least-once: process, then commit
options.pros: never loses
options.cons: a crash before commit replays some messages

options.name: exactly-once: idempotent producer + transactions that write outputs and offsets atomically
options.pros: no loss, no duplicates inside the system
options.cons: extra latency and coordination; only covers effects that go back into the log

deep_dives.choice: at-least-once by default with an idempotent producer (producer_id + per-partition sequence, so broker-side retries never duplicate); exactly-once via transactions as an opt-in for read-process-write pipelines
deep_dives.why: Most consumers write to external systems that need their own idempotency anyway; the idempotent producer removes the common duplicate source (retried produce) at almost no cost.

deep_dives.title: Push vs pull to consumers

options.name: broker pushes
options.pros: lowest latency when consumers keep up
options.cons: floods slow consumers; broker tracks each consumer's rate

options.name: consumer pulls with long-poll
options.pros: consumer controls pace and batch size; natural backpressure
options.cons: an empty poll costs a request (mitigated by max_wait)

deep_dives.why: Consumers at very different speeds read the same log; pull keeps the broker stateless about them and lets a lagging group catch up in big batches.

deep_dives.title: Hot partitions and choosing partition counts

options.name: few partitions per topic
options.pros: less metadata and fewer files
options.cons: throughput and consumer parallelism are capped

options.name: many partitions up front, sized for peak / per-partition throughput
options.pros: room to grow consumers without remapping keys
options.cons: more open files and longer elections

deep_dives.choice: size partitions for peak throughput ÷ ~10 MB/s per partition and for the max consumer count, with headroom; split hot keys by salting when per-key order allows
deep_dives.why: Adding partitions later changes key → partition mapping and breaks per-key order across the change, so pick generously; a single hot key is bounded by one partition's throughput.

deep_dives.title: Making the broker fast

options.name: per-message writes and reads through application buffers
options.pros: simple
options.cons: syscalls and copies per message

options.name: producer batching + compression, OS page cache, zero-copy sendfile to consumers
options.pros: few large sequential IOs; reads of recent data never touch disk
options.cons: batching adds a few ms of linger

deep_dives.choice: batch + compress in the producer, keep batches intact on disk, serve consumers with zero-copy from the page cache
deep_dives.why: N1 needs 1 GB/s with modest hardware; most consumers read the last few seconds, which are still in the page cache.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Hot partitions from skewed keys (bounded by one leader's disk and NIC), controller metadata for very high partition counts, consumer parallelism capped by partitions, rebalances pausing large groups.
wrapup.failures: Broker dies: controller elects new leaders from the ISR within seconds; producers retry (idempotent, no duplicates); consumers refetch metadata. Zone lost: RF 3 across zones keeps two copies, min ISR 2 still met. Slow follower: dropped from the ISR, writes continue. Consumer dies: coordinator reassigns its partitions; the new owner resumes from the committed offset (at-least-once replays).
wrapup.monitoring: Under-replicated and offline partitions, ISR shrink rate, produce/fetch latency p99, consumer lag per group (messages and seconds), disk usage vs retention, controller election count, request queue time.
wrapup.scale: Add brokers and move partitions onto them (throttled reassignment); add partitions for new parallelism (re-keying caveat); tiered storage for longer retention; separate clusters per domain for blast radius.
wrapup.future: Cross-region mirroring, delayed/scheduled messages, per-message acks (share groups) for queue-style work, a schema registry.
